extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, legal practitioners, and advanced law students working on patent transfers
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and criteria governing transfer/alienation of patents (assignments, grants, licenses) under U.S. law: definitions, who may transfer, to whom, form/recording requirements, and the substantive test for whether a conveyance transfers the monopoly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory modes of transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutes recognize only two modes by which the monopoly may be transferred, — one by a conveyance of the entire interest in the invention, or of an undivided part thereof, for the whole country; the other by a conveyance of a similar interest, or part interest, within some portion of the United States. ... The conveyance of the subordinate rights in the invention, either separately or united, without affecting the monopoly otherwise than by estoppel, is also permitted; ... custom and judicial sanction have attached the name of License.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies three functional forms encountered in practice: Assignment (entire/undivided interest across the United States), Grant (exclusive sectional/territorial right), and License (subordinate/non-transferring rights). Courts and statutes use these categories to determine rights and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment defined (territorial scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment is a transfer of the entire interest in a patented invention, or of an undivided portion of such entire interest, as to every section of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An assignment relates to the entire U.S. ownership (or an undivided part thereof). A conveyance that purports only to grant rights limited to particular territories or leaves exclusive rights in the transferor will not be an assignment for purposes of transferring the monopoly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of an assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: When the entire interest is assigned, it substitutes the assignee for the original patentee, conferring upon him, to their full extent, the rights embraced in the invention and the prohibitory powers bestowed by the patent. Where an undivided interest is transferred, it places the assignee upon an equality, in all respects, with his assignor and the original patentee, vesting in him complete but not exclusive rights and powers as to the monopoly and the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full assignment = assignee steps into patentee's shoes with full statutory rights (including injunctive relief). Assignment of undivided interest = co-ownership; each co-owner has powers and may assign his share.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between assignment, grant, and license (subject-matter/territorial test)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential difference between them consists in the territorial area to which they relate. An assignment transfers also some interest in the monopoly, while a license leaves the monopoly unaffected in the hands of the licensor, except that it cannot be enforced against the rights conferred by him upon the licensee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practical test: if the conveyance vests in the alienee the entire interest in the invention (or makes him a joint-owner) it transfers the monopoly and is an assignment; if it leaves any exclusive right in the alienor, or grants only non-exclusive/practice rights, it is a license. Grants are exclusive sectional rights limited to territory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive test: transfer of monopoly vs practice-rights
rubrics_metrics.description: If the conveyance vests in the alienee the entire interest in the invention, or if it makes him a joint-owner with the alienor in such entire interest, it transfers the monopoly to the same extent as the invention, and is an assignment. But if it leaves in the alienor any exclusive right whatever in the invention, ... the conveyance is a license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transfers of mere rights to 'make, use, and sell' for limited purposes or places, or non-exclusive rights, typically are licenses; transfer of exclusive rights (or undivided interest in exclusive rights) generally constitutes an assignment that transfers the monopoly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character of conveyance determined by subject-matter not by labels/terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The character of a conveyance, as thus determined by its subject-matter, cannot be varied by the terms and conditions upon which the transfer has been made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clauses typical of licenses (royalty provisions, forfeiture on breach, periodic payments) do not convert an assignment into a license if the subject-matter actually transfers an interest in the monopoly; look to substance over form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may make an assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment of a patented invention can be made only by one in whom the ownership of both the invention and the monopoly resides. At the outset this double ownership vests in the patentee ... Unless transferred by an assignment, or territorially divided by a grant, this ownership remains in him while living, and at his death passes to his executor or administrator as trustees for his heirs or devisees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the current legal owner of the patent/monopoly can effect a valid assignment of the legal title; successive assignments pass title along. Administrators/executors may act for deceased owners as provided by statute/local law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments when owner insolvent / involuntary alienation
rubrics_metrics.description: The ownership of a patented invention cannot be seized and sold on execution by a sheriff like a personal chattel, nor ... vest in a receiver or a trustee in insolvency by virtue of the judicial decree ... Neither a bankrupt court, nor a court of equity, nor any person acting under their authority, can affect the ownership of a patented invention without the actual or presumed co-operation of the individual in whom such ownership is vested by the issue of the patent or by assignment from the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent specific statutory authority or court orders compelling assignment, patents are not subject to ordinary involuntary alienation; courts may in equity compel transfers in limited circumstances, but title still derives from the owner.

rubrics_metrics.name: To whom an assignment may be made
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment of a patented invention may be made to any person without regard to age, capacity, or citizenship. A corporation may become the owner both of the invention and monopoly without receiving special charter-powers for that purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are minimal restrictions on assignee capacity; corporations and minors may be assignees (local law may govern capacity issues for certain actors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and general requisites of an assignment (writing, signature, operative words)
rubrics_metrics.description: No particular form for an assignment is prescribed. ... it must be made in writing and be signed by the assignors. It must also contain operative words unequivocally indicating an intention to convey an interest both in the invention and in the monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While formal statutory wording is unnecessary, the instrument must: comply with U.S. law, be written and signed by the owner(s), and clearly describe the interest conveyed (sufficient intelligible description of the patent or rights is required). Parol transfers do not convey legal title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written instrument required to convey legal title (vs parol/equitable rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: That the legal title to a patent can be transferred only by a written instrument, signed by the owner of the patent. ... A parol agreement to assign will pass an equitable title which a court of equity will enforce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parol agreements may create enforceable equitable obligations (and may allow an assignee to procure the patent in his name if carried out), but legal title requires a signed written transfer by the patent owner; equitable remedies exist for breach of parol promises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments of undivided interests and co-ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: That the assignment of an undivided interest makes the assignor and assignee joint-owners of the patent. ... An assignee of an undivided interest occupies the same position and enjoys the same rights as any of his predecessors or co-owners, and is entitled to all the privileges and is subject to obligations conferred or imposed by the statutes upon the patentee and his assignees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assigning an undivided share confers co-ownership; each co-owner may separately convey his share and has equivalent statutory rights, subject to normal rules of co-ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer of rights incident to assigned rights (e.g., right to use follows right to make and sell)
rubrics_metrics.description: That the assignment of the right to make and sell carries the right to use, and if exclusively passes the entire monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining what rights were intended to pass, courts interpret conveyances of the right to make/sell as encompassing the right to use; transferring exclusive make/sell rights will generally be treated as transferring the monopoly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording and statutory governance
rubrics_metrics.description: The assignment and also every grant and conveyance of the exclusive right under any patent ... shall be recorded. Assignments are governed wholly by statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments/grants affecting exclusive rights are subject to recording requirements under the patent statutes; statutory provisions control assignability, recording, and many consequences of transfers—check applicable recording/notice rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on form-based shortcuts and agent signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: That an assignment executed by an attorney must be signed with name of the principal and sealed with his seal. That an assignment by an attorney in his own name is invalid; the signature of the owner being essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the written instrument bears the owner's signature (or authorized execution in the owner's name), and follow formalities required by local practice (seals where required). Instruments styled as certificates or promises to transfer are not assignments unless intended and executed to convey title.
